look_here_first: HAIRY WOOLLYGRASS — SHORT, UPRIGHT WHITE HEADS ABOVE A LOW TUFT. Look for a small warm-season perennial clump, often 10–30 cm tall on shallow limestone or gravel, with tight narrow folded leaves bearing pale/white hardened margins. Thin, mostly leafless flower stalks rise above the basal blades, ending in small dense pale-to-purplish, club-shaped heads of SEVERAL closely packed, woolly spikelets. A mature spikelet typically has 4–12 florets in the UT Williamson County material; each fertile lemma has THREE hairy veins, fine long hairs below, a tiny apical notch and ONE short awn. The two relatively smooth glumes are SHORTER than the lowermost floret. The true leaf collar LIGULE IS A FRINGE OF HAIRS (very short in the UT local treatment), NOT a large membrane. Confirm the glumes/lemma/awn under 10–20×, not from an overview photo.

best_field_traits: LOW PERENNIAL TUFT: usually 10–30 cm, sometimes to ~40 cm; dry limestone/caliche/gravel. Seasonal short stature and habitat support recognition, not precise ID.
LEAVES: mostly basal, narrow often folded along the midvein; notably white, stiff/cartilaginous margins and sharply pointed blade tip, best checked with a lens.
FLOWERING STALKS: upright thin and mostly leafless above the basal blades; individual compact club-shaped or short cylindrical tuft-like heads at their tips.

HEAD: a condensed group of about 3–10 closely placed separate spikelets in local UT material; often whitish to purplish depending on development. Do not confuse these spikelets with individual florets.
SPIKELETS: local mature examples typically 6–11 mm with 4–12 FLORETS EACH (elsewhere higher counts reported), laterally compressed and conspicuously silky.
GLUMES: two rather smooth, often one-veined bracts, SHORTER than the lowermost floret; woolly lemma hairs should NOT be misassigned to the glumes.
LEMMAS: three-nerved with soft pilose hairs below and along the nerves, shallowly notched at tip (~0–0.5 mm notch), and one tiny awn roughly 0.5–2.5 mm. This needs a 10–20× dissection.
LIGULE: small FRINGE OF HAIRS at actual inner leaf-collar, not a membrane; distinguish long collar hairs from the much shorter true ligule.
WARNING: photograph alone does not establish the presence/number of lemma veins, glume proportions, awn insertions or a locality-native PASS.
what_to_photograph_for_confirmation: FULL SAME-PLANT SERIES: entire rooted low clump, one mostly leafless stalk and its attached club-shaped head, with 1-cm ruler and site context.
LEAF BLADE 10×: folded along raised keel, the pair of pale cartilaginous margins, and pointed prowlike tip with a millimeter scale.
TRUE COLLAR 20×: hair-fringe ligule (UT Williamson treatment up to ~0.35 mm) separately from longer COLLAR hairs, with 1-mm scale; no membranous ligule label.
ONE INTACT MATURE SPIKELET 10–20×: approximately 6–11 mm in UT Williamson material, with 4–12 florets counted inside it, two glumes exposed and scale.
GLUMES VS LEMMA 20×: demonstrate the TWO relatively glabrous shorter glumes and a separate THREE-NERVED hairy fertile lemma, with hairs correctly attached to the lemma veins.
LEMMA TIP 20×: show a shallow notch (0.5 mm or less) and one tiny awn (often around 0.5–2.5 mm), with measurement; match E. avenaceum deeper notch under the same scale.
PALEA / HAIR DETAIL 20×: isolate a true two-veined palea and its hairy keel from a fertile floret without misidentifying neighboring spikelet bracts.
crew_field_check: Look for the whole low plant: tight heads raised on thin stalks above a separate tufted base, NOT woolly foliage spreading flat on the ground.
At the blade base distinguish true ligule HAIR FRINGE from much longer exterior collar hairs. Do not copy membrane-based grass keys to this species.
Under 10–20× pick one mature spikelet: count FLORETS inside it, then identify two relatively bare shorter glumes, hairy 3-nerved lemma, shallow notch and one small awn.

Compare Munroa pulchella (flowerheads buried among ground-level pointed leaf clusters), Tridens texanus (separated hanging spikelets on OPEN flexible panicle branches), and Erioneuron avenaceum (deeper lemma notch, longer glume).
Keep unverified sterile grass labelled Erioneuron cf. pilosum or grass sp.; do not claim this is finished merely because several legitimate photographs are installed.

comparisons.key_distinctions: FLUFFGRASS / Munroa pulchella (syn. Dasyochloa pulchella): hugs the ground as a radiating, sometimes stoloniferous, very low spiky mat; dense woolly spikelet packets nest DOWN among pungent pointed leaves, not atop long mostly leafless erect stalks. TEXAS TRIDENS / Tridens texanus: a more open/flexuous branched panicle with spaced, hanging multiple-flowered spikelets and often bare lower portions of its panicle branches; it is NOT the short dense club of Erioneuron. LARGE-FLOWERED WOOLLYGRASS / Erioneuron avenaceum: can also carry stalked compact woolly heads; in a mature dissection the lemma notch is DEEPER (about 1–2.5 mm) and its upper glume often reaches or passes the lowest floret, compared with E. pilosum's shallow ~0–0.5 mm notch and both glumes shorter than the lowest floret. GENERAL THREEAWNS / Aristida spp.: three long awn limbs arise from one lemma, unlike hairy woollygrass's one short awn. Color, white hairs, dry gravel habitat and tuft height alone cannot decide identity.

reconciliation_20261022.look_here_first: Low perennial tuft with pale narrow club-shaped heads on mostly leafless upright stalks; distinguish woolly spikelet packets from ground-hugging Munroa pulchella.

measured_species_finalization_20261024.look_here_first: HAIRY WOOLLYGRASS: tiny perennial basal tuft with folded white-edged blades and short dense woolly spikelets RAISED on mostly leafless stalks. Confirm under 10–20×: two relatively smooth short 1-veined glumes, multiple florets with 3-veined hairy lemmas, shallow notched tips and ONE short awn per fertile lemma; a true fringe-of-hairs ligule, not a long membranous flap.
measured_diagnostic_key: GROWTH: perennial tuft; Kew reports culms 10–30 cm, folded narrow blades 2–8(–11) cm long and 1–2 mm wide with firm pale/cartilaginous margins. The raised short dense head differs from Munroa's woolly spikelet clusters nested among ground-level pointed leaves.

COLLAR/LIGULE: true ligule is a HAIR FRINGE. Kew GrassBase describes ~0.5 mm; the Smithsonian Mexico grass treatment gives 2–3.5 mm, while an existing local UT treatment cited in this card describes a much shorter fringe (~0.35 mm). These treatments disagree: DO NOT use a single ligule length as a species threshold or relabel the ligule as a membrane. Photograph actual blade/sheath junction and separate longer collar hairs.

PANICLE: Kew GrassBase describes a compact oval head ~2–3 cm long and ~1.5–2 cm wide with about 4–9 spikelets; Smithsonian reports ~1–4(6) cm panicles with 3–9 shortly pedicelled spikelets. Each spikelet is NOT one floret.

SPIKELETS: Kew reports 10–16 mm and 7–18 fertile florets; Smithsonian reports 6–12(15) mm and (5)6–12(20) florets. Older local UT treatment in this card gives roughly 6–11 mm and 4–12 florets. These are published populations/treatments, not image-measured values; count and measure one ripe spikelet.

GLUMES: two similar persistent, relatively smooth 1-veined glumes; Kew describes lower and upper ~4.5–6 mm, generally shorter than full spikelet. Distinguish glumes from individual hairy florets; glume length versus lowest floret may overlap and must be examined in a mature specimen.

FERTILE LEMMA: Kew ~4.5–6 mm, three-veined and hairy along nerves/edges, apex shallowly notched; one short awn (~1–2 mm Kew; ~0.5–2.5 mm Smithsonian) emerges from the notch SINUS. Do not mistake numerous floret awns for three awns on a single lemma.
PALEA: two-veined, approximately half the lemma length in Kew; palea keels ciliate, back hairy. Requires actual dissected floret, not an overview head image.
central_texas_lookalikes: Munroa pulchella (fluffgrass): ground-hugging, pointed leaf clusters enclosing woolly flower packets rather than elevated terminal woolly clubs; verify crown/head attachment.
Tridentopsis mutica (slim tridens): taller narrow contracted spike-like panicle with multiple florets, but no identical short woolly head and white-edged leaf combination; check lemma nerve hairs.
Tridens texanus (Texas tridens): open branching panicle with spaced spikelets; check whole head before dissection.
Erioneuron avenaceum (comparison only): deeper lemma-tip notch and upper glume often reaching lowest floret; cannot separate on woolly color alone.
Aristida spp. (threeawns): three awn limbs on a SINGLE lemma rather than one short awn arising from one notched lemma.

field_photo_quickcheck.heading: Hairy tridens — woolly head above the leaf tuft, then inspect one floret
steps: FIELD HABIT FIRST: use Tom Chester's credited whole in-ground Arizona photo to follow the leafy cluster at ground level up the flowering culm to a compact woolly head. The root attachment is not exposed.
WHITE LEAF EDGE NEXT: his close foliage photograph shows really pale white margins of narrow folded blades and crowded basal tillers, not a peeled-open inner ligule.
FLORAL HAIRS NEXT: his close head shows silvery woolly hair and many pointed overlapping floret/spikelet parts; inspect real leaves and head together rather than identifying generic blond fluff.

START at the three already archived Joey Santore views: follow the short basal folded leaf tuft to distinct mostly bare flowering culms, each ending in a tight pale woolly head; the overall structure, not woolliness alone, is the first clue.

ZOOM into existing Joey photo 202577165 to recognize overlapping spikelets and projecting hairs. Existing arrows correctly label visible silky fringes only, NOT particular glumes, lemmas or measured hairs.

COMPARE one mature spikelet at a millimeter scale. The local Williamson County treatment describes mostly 6–11 mm spikelets bearing 4–12 fertile florets, while broader GrassBase describes 10–16 mm and 7–18 florets. Different samples/ranges are not proof of a wrong identification.

DISSECT two relatively smooth persistent one-veined glumes and a three-veined, conspicuously pilose fertile lemma. Verify that the lemma tip has one short awn and a notch not more than about 0.5 mm deep; compare the deeper notch in E. avenaceum.
OPEN a basal leaf collar at 20×: distinguish the very short ~0.35 mm HAIR-FRINGE LIGULE from collar hairs that may exceed 1 mm; photograph attachment points and 1-mm scale.

COMPARE the different-species panels: Munroa pulchella holds its woolly structures low among pointed leaves, and Tridens texanus has a loose branched flowering head, unlike the elevated compact Erioneuron cluster.
HOLD anatomical completion until an authenticated same-plant series shows the folded white-edged leaf, ligule, dissected glumes and hairy lemma plus notch/one short awn with scale.
field_photo_quickcheck.field_rule: Compact white/purplish woolly heads on slender largely bare flowering culms ABOVE a low tuft of folded white-edged leaves; verify smooth short glumes versus a THREE-NERVED hairy one-awned lemma.
field_photo_quickcheck.warning: Four original image records remain unchanged: three physically hosted Joey source views retain CC BY-NC 4.0 and one user-owned Calvin King image retains its private-use restriction. The user-owned photo has NOT been promoted to the public panel. 3 exact species panels + 2 explicitly different-species comparison panels; no newly sourced anatomy JPEG, no fabricated arrow. Report local-versus-broad measurements without collapsing biological variation into one asserted photo measurement. 2026-10-26: three additional real source-identifed Tom Chester photographs were individually verified for explicit credited reproduction, physically archived and added as whole in-ground bunch, white-edged basal blades and woolly spikelet head with six new gross arrows. No actual exposed 0.35-mm inner ligule or scale; no underground root system. Keep user's private-only Calvin King original OUT of the gallery; preserve Joey NC photo-level terms.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 01 · RAISED WOOLLY HEADS
field_id_short_tiles.short: Short dense pale heads stand above a low leafy tuft
field_id_short_tiles.details: A perennial of dry limestone or gravel, often 10–30 cm tall. Slender, mostly leafless stalks carry compact oval or club-shaped clusters of several spikelets ABOVE a basal fan of folded narrow leaves. The existing three Joey Santore source-identified panels show the silhouette, not a measured root connection or microscopic bracts.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 02 · FOLDED WHITE-EDGED BLADES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Narrow folded leaves with stiff pale margins
field_id_short_tiles.details: Look at the basal leaf blades, typically 1–2 mm wide in Kew's description, often folded with whitish firm/cartilaginous margins and pointed tips. These help separate the small tuft from loose-leaved tridens, but no current gallery photo measures the actual margin, keel or width. Photograph the same plant at 10× with a millimeter bar.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 03 · FIND THE TRUE HAIR LIGULE
field_id_short_tiles.short: Hair fringe at the INNER blade–sheath junction, not a broad membrane
field_id_short_tiles.details: Open the true collar and distinguish the ligule hair fringe from longer adjacent collar hairs. Published treatments disagree on fringe length: about 0.35 mm in the local UT account, ~0.5 mm in Kew GrassBase, and 2–3.5 mm in another regional treatment. Do not force one threshold or point an arrow at unexposed collar hairs. A measured inner-collar macro is still missing.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 04 · COUNT FLORETS INSIDE ONE SPIKELET
field_id_short_tiles.short: Several woolly spikelets per head; multiple florets per spikelet
field_id_short_tiles.details: One terminal head contains several separate spikelets; each spikelet in turn contains many florets. Published mature spikelet lengths range about 6–16 mm across regional treatments, with local UT examples around 6–11 mm and 4–12 florets; broader treatments report more. Expose and count florets in ONE intact ripe spikelet. The current head macro cannot prove those counts.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 05 · GLUMES VS HAIRY LEMMA
field_id_short_tiles.short: Two relatively smooth 1-veined glumes; hairy 3-veined fertile lemmas
field_id_short_tiles.details: Separate the two persistent glumes from a fertile floret. Kew describes glumes roughly 4.5–6 mm and fertile lemmas roughly 4.5–6 mm, with three hairy nerves, a shallow notch and ONE short awn (local account often ~0.5–2.5 mm). Measure the actual lemma notch and awn insertion under 10–20×. Silky hairs visible in a crowded head must NOT automatically be labeled as glume hairs.

field_id_short_tiles.heading: 06 · CHECK THE LOOK-ALIKES
field_id_short_tiles.short: Raised woolly club ≠ ground-level fluffgrass; one awn ≠ threeawn
field_id_short_tiles.details: Munroa pulchella packs woolly units DOWN among sharply pointed ground-level leaves, unlike the raised Erioneuron head. Tridens texanus has a loose branched panicle with separated hanging spikelets. Erioneuron avenaceum requires dissection: its lemma notch is generally deeper (~1–2.5 mm versus ~0–0.5 mm in the local E. pilosum account), and its upper glume may reach the lowermost floret. Aristida has three awn limbs from one lemma. Keep uncertain sterile plants provisional.
